procedural_history.originating_court: High Court of Judicature at Madras
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 24.02.2016 of the High Court of Judicature at Madras in HCP No. 2442 of 2015
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court of Judicature at Madras issued a judgment and order in H.C.P. No. 2442/2015 on February 24, 2016.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Government of Tamil Nadu appealed the High Court's judgment and order to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court disposed of the appeal.

directions: The Judgment of the Court is set aside.
As a consequence, the detention order dated 31 August 2015 bearing G.O. No. SR.1/63-5/2015 Public (SC) Department shall stand revived.
However, since the period of detention has come to an end, nothing further remains except for this Court to clarify the true legal position as we have done in the above terms.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court should correct an incorrect statement of legal position by the High Court, even when the period of detention has already ended, rendering the appeal moot in a practical sense.

facts: The High Court quashed an order of detention because the order did not specify the period of detention.
By the time the appeal reached the Supreme Court, the period of detention had already come to an end, making the appeal moot in a practical sense.
The High Court had based its decision on a previous Supreme Court case, *Bhiryani*.
law: The Supreme Court has a duty to clarify the correct legal position, even if the specific case has become moot.
The legal precedent established in *Bhiryani* was overruled by a larger, three-judge bench in the case of *T Devaki v Government of Tamil Nadu*.
The correct legal principle, as established in *Devaki* and other cases, is that a detention order is not rendered illegal or invalid merely because it does not specify the period of detention.
application: The Supreme Court acknowledged that the detention period had ended but accepted the submission that it was necessary to correct the High Court's incorrect statement of the law.
The Court found that the High Court was not justified in its decision because it had relied on the *Bhiryani* case, which was no longer good law.
The Court applied the correct precedent from the larger bench in *Devaki*, stating that the High Court's reasoning did not reflect the correct legal position.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that it should correct the High Court's incorrect statement of the legal position. It held that even though the detention period had ended, it was necessary to clarify that a detention order is not illegal simply because it fails to specify the detention period, thereby setting aside the High Court's erroneous legal reasoning.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court should correct an incorrect statement of legal position by the High Court, even when the period of detention has already ended, rendering the appeal moot in a practical sense.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that even though the period of detention had concluded, it was necessary for the Court to correct the incorrect statement of the legal position made by the High Court.
The appellant's counsel highlighted that the High Court had relied on a decision (Bhiryani) that was previously overruled by a larger bench in T Devaki v Government of Tamil Nadu.

statutes.act_name: Conservation of Foreign Exchange and Prevention of Smuggling Activities Act, 1974
Jammu and Kashmir Preventive Detention Act, 1964

cases.case_name: T Devaki v. Government of Tamil Nadu
cases.principle: Since legislation does not require the detaining authority to specify the period for which a detenue is required to be detained, the order of detention is not rendered invalid or illegal in the absence of such specification.

cases.case_name: Ujagar Singh v. State of Punjab
cases.principle: Non-specification of any definite period in a detention order made under Section 3 of the Preventive Detention Act, 1950 was not a material omission rendering the order invalid.

cases.case_name: Suna Ullah Butt v. State of Jammu & Kashmir
cases.principle: Since the State Government had power to revoke or modify the detention order at any time before the completion of the maximum period, it was not necessary for the State Government to specify the period of detention.

cases.case_name: Suresh Bhojraj Chelani v. State of Maharashtra
cases.principle: The COFEPOSA Act did not require the detaining authority to mention the period of detention in the order of detention.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An order of detention is not rendered illegal merely because it does not specify the period of detention.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Supreme Court concluded that it is necessary to correct an incorrect statement of the legal position made by a High Court, even when the specific controversy has become moot (in this case, because the period of detention had ended). The High Court erred by relying on a decision of a two-judge bench in Bhiryani, which had been explicitly overruled by a larger three-judge bench in T Devaki v Government of Tamil Nadu. Therefore, the Court set aside the High Court's judgment to clarify the true legal position for future guidance.
legal_tests_applied: The court applied the doctrine of precedent (stare decisis), enforcing the rule that a decision by a larger bench of the Supreme Court overrules a conflicting decision by a smaller bench, and that High Courts are bound by the ruling of the larger bench.
policy_considerations: The court's intervention, despite the mootness of the appeal, was driven by the systemic need to maintain a correct and consistent body of law. The court acted to prevent an incorrect legal precedent set by the High Court from being followed in future cases, thereby ensuring legal certainty and the proper administration of justice.
